latin: Genovefā. — Quae mihi explānāvistī, ea ad tōtum librum legendum mē hortantur. Vīsne mihi eum commodāre?
Albertus. — Libentissimē. Cum domum intrāvistī, ultimam pāginam legēbam. Ecce liber!
Gen. — Ēditiō pulcherrima est. Quis illās lepidās imāginēs colōribus jūcundīs pīnxit<sup>1</sup>?
Alb. — Auctor ipse; simpliciter sed lepidē delineābat.
Gen. — Crēdisne mē exemplar latīnum intellegere posse*?
Alb. — Profectō potes*. Sed ēn tibi exemplar<sup>2</sup> linguā nostrā scrīptum. Quantum fierī potest, cave nē eō ūtāris, nisi in summā difficultāte.
Gen. — Grātiās tibi agō. Cōnsiliō tuō<sup>3</sup> ūtar.
Alb. — Nē tamen lēctiōnēs quotīdiānās discere discōsque audīre oblīta sīs!
Octo post diēbus: Gen. — Librum sine magnā difficultāte latīne scrīptum legī. Glossāriō paululum ūsa sum.
In fīne latīnum cum exemplārī linguā nostrā scrīptō contulī<sup>4</sup>. Nōn crēdēbam linguam patriam in latīnam tantā simplicitāte convertī posse*.
Alb. — Eugē! Optimum invēnistī modum linguārum externārum discendārum, tot librōs legendō<sup>5</sup> quot<sup>6</sup> possibile est.
Gen. — Sōla difficultās in inceptū est. Initiō paene nihil intellegis.
Alb. — Hoc ipsō tempore pergendum est<sup>7</sup>. Prīmum legere atque etiam legere oportet*, sine glossāriī ūsū.
Tunc auctōris stilō paulātim insuescis, et paulātim melius meliusque ejus linguam intellegis.
Gen. — Habēsne alterum librum parī difficultāte?
Alb. — Tibi librum anglicum commodābō, quī et puerīs scrīptus est. Sed nunc cēnātum eāmus*!
latinAccented: Genóvefā. — Quae mihi explānāvístī, ea ad tōtum librum legéndum mē hortántur. Vīsne mihi eum commodā́re?
Albértus. — Libentíssimē. Cum domum intrāvístī, últimam pā́ginam legḗbam. Ecce liber!
Gen. — Ēdítiō pulchérrima est. Quis illās lépidās imā́ginēs colṓribus jūcúndīs pīnxit<sup>1</sup>?
Alb. — Auctor ipse; simplíciter sed lépidē delineā́bat.
Gen. — Crēdísne mē exémplar latī́num intellégere posse*?
Alb. — Proféctō potes*. Sed ēn tibi exémplar<sup>2</sup> linguā nostrā scrīptum. Quantum fíerī potest, cave nē eō ūtā́ris, nisi in summā difficultā́te.
Gen. — Grā́tiās tibi agō. Cōnsíliō tuō<sup>3</sup> ūtar.
Alb. — Nē tamen lēctiṓnēs quotīdiā́nās díscere discṓsque audī́re oblī́ta sīs!
Octo post diḗbus: Gen. — Librum sine magnā difficultā́te latī́ne scrīptum legī. Glossā́riō páululum ūsa sum.
In fīne latī́num cum exemplā́rī linguā nostrā scrīptō cóntulī<sup>4</sup>. Nōn crēdḗbam linguam pátriam in latī́nam tantā simplicitā́te convértī posse*.
Alb. — Éugē! Óptimum invēnístī modum linguā́rum externā́rum discendā́rum, tot librōs legéndō<sup>5</sup> quot<sup>6</sup> possíbile est.
Gen. — Sōla difficúltās in incéptū est. Inítiō paene nihil intéllegis.
Alb. — Hoc ipsō témpore pergéndum est<sup>7</sup>. Prīmum légere atque étiam légere opórtet*, sine glossā́riī ūsū.
Tunc auctṓris stilō paulā́tim insuéscis, et paulā́tim mélius meliúsque ejus linguam intéllegis.
Gen. — Habḗsne álterum librum parī difficultā́te?
Alb. — Tibi librum ánglicum commodā́bō, quī et púerīs scrīptus est. Sed nunc cēnā́tum eā́mus*!
english: Geneviève. — [What] (those things) you have just explained to me [makes] me want to read the whole book. Do you want to lend it to me?
Albert. — Very willingly. When you came into the house, I was reading the last page. Here is the book!
Gen. — The edition is very beautiful. Who [did] these pretty pictures in pleasant colours (painted)?
Alb. — The author himself; he drew very simply but pleasantly.
Gen. — Do you think that I can understand the copy in Latin?
Alb. — Certainly you can. But here for you is a copy in our language (written). Try not to use it, except [if you are] in very great difficulty.
Gen. — I thank you; I [will follow] (will make use of) your advice.
Alb. — [Don't forget] (subj. pft) however to study the daily lessons and to listen to the records!
Eight days later: Gen. — I read the book without great difficulty in Latin. I used the dictionary a little.

To finish, I compared [the copy] in Latin [with that] (with copy) written [in] our language. I did not think that [our] mother tongue could [so simply] (with such simplicity) be translated into Latin.
Alb. — Hurrah! You have found the best means of learning foreign languages, by reading as many books as possible (is).
Gen. — The only difficulty is in the beginning. At the start [one] (you) understand(s) almost nothing.
Alb. — It is at that very moment that one must persevere. First one must read and read again, without using the dictionary.
Then little by little you get used to the author's style, and little by little you understand his language better and better.
Gen. — Do you have another book of equal difficulty?
Alb. — I will lend you an English book, which was also written for children. But now let's go and have dinner!

footnotes: Pingo, -is, -ere, pinxi, pictum, to paint, to draw; and, figuratively, to describe; pictor, -oris, the painter; pictura, -ae, f., painting.
Exemplar, -aris, n., is declined like a parisyllabic (like mare, maris, n.: abl. sg. in i and gen. pl. in ium). The same goes for words in al and ar, which were formerly in ale and are.

Consilium, advice; not to be confused with concilium, the council, the assembly. There is moreover no risk of error if you pronounce the latter correctly: «konnkilioumm» (or in the Italian way «konntchilioumm»).
Conferre*, to gather, to compare, is another compound of ferre.

Up to now we have met the verbal adjective much more often than the gerund. With the gerund, we have:
1° Accusative: te hortor ad discendum (linguas), I exhort you to learn (languages).
2° Genitive: modus discendi (linguas), a means of learning (languages).
3° Dative, ablative: discendo (linguas), for learning (dat.), by learning (abl.) (languages); likewise libros legendo.

When the gerund has a complement (linguas in our example), Latin preferably uses the verbal adjective, which then agrees with this complement; our three turns of phrase become, while keeping the same sense:
1° Accusative: te hortor ad linguas discendas;
2° Genitive: modus linguarum discendarum;
3° Dative and ablative: linguis discendis.

Tot... quot, indeclinable, are used for things (or beings) that one can count, whereas tantus, -a, -um and quantus, -a, -um are used for things more or less large. Tot homines quot sententiae!, as many people, as many opinions! But (L. 74, P. 5): tantum... exigendum est quantum unusquisque dare potest.
Pergo, -is, -ere, perrexi, perrectum, to continue on one's way, to continue.
comments: Verber, -eris, n., blow (of the whip). — Pronus, -a, -um, leaning. — Clamitare, frequentative of clamare (to cry), to cry without stopping. Likewise below agitare, frequentative of agere. — Ferus, -a, -um, wild, ferocious, savage; fera, -ae, f., wild beast, wild animal. — Factio, -onis, f., action or power of doing (facere), position (political), party, clan, faction. — Cingo, -is, -ere, cinxi, cinctum, to gird, to surround; here in the passive. — Rem facere, to earn money, to make one's fortune, corresponds to the first sense of res, rei, f., which, like the French chose, has become in the long run a word for EVERYTHING (OMNIBUS)!

Russatus, -a, -um, dark red. As in our time, one recognized racers by the colour of their jersey, and each colour had its partisans, that is to say a «faction». — Venetus, -a, -um, sea blue, colour of the Veneti (Veneti), inhabitants of Venetia (Venetia) and of the faction of the «blues». — Prasinus, -a, -um, green, colour of a 3rd faction. — Fiscus, -i, m., wicker basket; by extension, the money that one gathers in it, the public treasury, the fisc. — Fors, fortis, f., chance; fortuitus, -a, -um, accidental, fortuitous.
More than one emperor was passionate about horses and charioteers. Caligula (12-41 A.D.) loved «the greens» to the point of spending whole days with them.

latin: Dum in verbera
Prōnus pendeō
Clāmitat fera
Nostra factiō.
Cingor laureīs;
Laetor prīncipem
Nostrīs dē victōriīs
Magnam fēcisse rem.
Prīnceps semper sim!
Nīl praetereat*!
Quis sīc habet vim?
Quis sīc agitat?
Sit russātō mors!
Tremat venetus!
Fiscō tamen favet fors
Cum vincit prasinus.

english: While over the whip(s)
— leaning [I hang on] (I hang)
— our party
— utters wild cries.
I am crowned with laurels;
— I rejoice [that the emperor] (prince)
— thanks to our victories
— has won a lot of money.
May I always be first!
— May nothing get past me!
— Who has such strength?
— Who drives thus?
Death to the red!
— May the blue tremble!
— Chance however favours the treasury (dative)
— when the green wins.
